p1.title: Passage 1
paras: A modern office worker rarely spends more than a few minutes on a task before something interrupts it. A message arrives, a colleague leans over with a question, a reminder announces a meeting. Each interruption seems trivial, and most are answered within a minute. The real cost lies elsewhere. Studies of attention suggest that after a person switches away from a demanding task, it can take a considerable time to return to the depth of concentration that was lost, and that part of the mind remains occupied with the abandoned task even while it attends to the new one. A day broken into fragments may therefore be busy from morning to evening and yet produce little work of lasting value.

Organisations often treat this as a problem of individual discipline, urging employees to manage their time better. But the habits of a workplace are collective. If a reply within minutes is expected, no single worker can afford to switch off notifications without seeming negligent. Some firms have experimented with protected hours during which meetings are forbidden and messages need not be answered, and they report that difficult tasks are completed sooner. The lesson is not that communication is harmful, but that uninterrupted time is a resource, and like any resource it must be deliberately protected if it is not to be spent without notice.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The rapid growth of India’s digital economy, anchored by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and cheap mobile data, has turned the nation into a global blueprint for digital financial inclusion. By building a public digital infrastructure, the state has democratized electronic payments, allowing street vendors and major corporations alike to operate on the exact same interoperable network. This digital pivot has formalized large sectors of the informal economy, expanded fintech innovation, and streamlined direct benefit transfers, cutting out corruption. However, this sudden transition introduces severe economic vulnerabilities, notably an alarming escalation in sophisticated cyber-fraud and digital phishing operations targeting newly connected, digitally illiterate populations. Furthermore, the rapid growth of fintech lenders using predatory automated algorithms risks driving low-income borrowers into deep debt traps through high-interest short-term loans. The long-term stability of India's digital marketplace depends on implementing strong data protection laws, enforcing strict algorithm auditing for fintech firms, and launching massive public digital literacy campaigns.

opts: The hidden cost of interruptions and the need to protect focused time collectively.
The design of modern office buildings.
The rudeness of colleagues who interrupt one another.
The advantages of answering messages quickly.
questions.why: Main idea: interruptions have a 'real cost' and 'uninterrupted time is a resource' to be 'deliberately protected'.

questions.q: According to studies of attention, after switching away from a demanding task:
opts: Concentration returns at once.
The worker becomes more creative.
Part of the mind stays occupied with the abandoned task.
The worker forgets the task entirely.
questions.why: Detail: 'part of the mind remains occupied with the abandoned task even while it attends to the new one'.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, can a single worker not solve the problem alone?
opts: Shared expectations of quick replies make individual withdrawal look negligent.
Notifications cannot be switched off on office devices.
Individual workers lack any time-management skills.
Managers forbid workers from working alone.
questions.why: Inference: 'the habits of a workplace are collective... no single worker can afford to switch off notifications without seeming negligent'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards workplace communication is that it:
opts: Is irrelevant to the quality of work.
Is useful, but must be balanced against protected, uninterrupted time.
Should be as rapid and constant as possible.
Is harmful and should be largely abolished.
questions.why: Attitude: 'The lesson is not that communication is harmful, but that uninterrupted time is a resource'.

questions.q: The word "trivial" in the passage most nearly means:
opts: Of little importance
Rude
Difficult
Frequent
questions.why: Vocabulary: each interruption 'seems trivial' because it is answered within a minute.

questions.q: India's public digital infrastructure is credited with transforming the economy by
opts: shutting down informal street vending to protect large corporations
democratizing electronic payments across both informal and corporate sectors
forcing all fintech innovations under state-owned monopolies
eliminating the need for data protection laws
questions.why: Street vendors and corporations use “the exact same interoperable network”. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: According to the text, a direct benefit of formalising the informal economy through digital tools is
opts: the complete eradication of automated lending algorithms
streamlining direct benefit transfers and reducing corruption
eliminating the need for digital literacy campaigns
reducing the market share of major payment providers
questions.why: Stated in the third sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The author warns that newly connected, digitally illiterate populations are particularly vulnerable to
opts: strict data protection enforcement by the state
sophisticated cyber-fraud and digital phishing
removal of short-term fintech credit
network blackouts caused by UPI
questions.why: Stated in the fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: A major risk of automated fintech lending algorithms, per the passage, is that they can
opts: block low-income borrowers from electronic payments
drop interest rates so low that banks fail
drive low-income borrowers into debt traps through predatory short-term loans
crash the UPI architecture
questions.why: Stated in the fifth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The author concludes that the lasting success of India's digital marketplace requires
opts: phasing out UPI and returning to cash
letting fintech firms self-regulate
strong data laws, algorithm audits and mass digital literacy campaigns
restricting digital access to educated urban users
questions.why: The last sentence lists all three. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.
